01 — The Project

One reality, many ways of seeing it.

Quantum Worldviews studies what quantum science means for how human beings understand reality, meaning and the sacred.

Quantum mechanics long ago escaped the laboratory. Its language now shapes how people think about consciousness, freedom, chance and God — a conviction that the world is "quantum all the way up." Based at the University of Oxford's Ian Ramsey Centre, the project brings physicists, philosophers, theologians and social scientists into one conversation, and carries that conversation to the wider public through a podcast, documentaries, a newsletter and more.

Science

The physics as it actually is — rigorous, current, honestly represented, never mysticism in a lab coat.

Philosophy

Interpretation and metaphysics — what the mathematics could mean, and the limits of what it can settle.

Religion

Meaning, theology and the sacred — taking the questions of faith as seriously as the equations.

02 — The Logo

A spectrum, split from one light.

The Q is drawn as cloud-chamber particle tracks — the curving trails a charged particle leaves as it moves — resolving into a luminous ring with a flourishing tail. Many colours, one white light broken into a spectrum: many worldviews, one reality.

QUANTUMWORLDVIEWS
University of Oxford  |  Ian Ramsey Centre
Science · Philosophy · Religion

Anatomy

Concentric tracks form the ring, each ending in a particle dot. A quill tail sweeps down and flicks out, opening the ring so it reads as a Q. In the wordmark the round Q of QUANTUM sits directly over the O of WORLDVIEWS — observer and observed, two linked lenses.

Construction

Built as clean vector strokes — every track, dot and tail strand is a single continuous line, so the mark scales from a favicon to a building banner without losing its delicacy. The colour order rotates through the full spectrum around the ring.

03 — Lockups

Four ways to sign it.

Use the stacked lockup as the primary. Reach for the others when the space or the context calls for it.

The wordmark may also be set on its own as a running header. Full editable files for every lockup ship in the logo pack.

04 — Colourways

Made to work anywhere.

Full-colour is the hero, on near-black. On light backgrounds the line colours deepen and the glow is dropped. One-colour white and black cover everything else.

05 — Clear space & misuse

Give it room; keep it whole.

Clear space: keep a margin of at least the ring's stroke gap (≈ one quarter of the mark's height) free of other elements on all sides. Minimum sizes: mark 24px, full lockup 120px wide on screen.

✕Don't recolour the spectral tracks or reorder the hues.
✕Don't stretch, rotate or condense the mark.
✕Don't add drop shadows, outlines or extra glow.
✕Don't place full-colour on a busy photo — use white or black.
✕Don't swap the typefaces or re-space the wordmark.
✕Don't box the logo or fill the ring.

08 — Graphic language

Tracks, dots and light.

Beyond the logo, the particle track is the brand's signature device: fine luminous curves that end in a dot, a spectral hairline, or a soft radial halo behind a focal point. Use them sparingly — one gesture per surface.

The spectral bar — a full-width rule of the eight hues — marks major divisions and headers.

A single spectral gradient hairline is the quieter divider for inside a page or email.

09 — Voice & tone

Rigorous, curious, hospitable.

We take both the science and the questions of meaning seriously. We explain without dumbing down, hold tension without collapsing it, and never sell wonder we can't back up.

"Quantum all the way up" — and all the way in.

We do

  • Write in plain, precise language a curious non-specialist can follow.
  • Represent the physics accurately, and mark where interpretation begins.
  • Give science, philosophy and faith a fair hearing at the same table.
  • Invite the reader in with real questions, not settled answers.

We don't

  • Sell "quantum healing", quantum mysticism, or hype.
  • Hide behind jargon or equations to sound authoritative.
  • Flatten the debate to a single winning view.
  • Mock belief, or dress speculation up as established fact.

11 — Team portraits

Faces, in the spectrum.

Contributor headshots use one system: a rich duotone in a single arc colour, a spectral ring echoing the Q, and a soft hue halo so hair melts into light rather than a hard cut-out. Every portrait is aligned to a common eye-line and matched head size, and lit from the same direction.

The recipe

Desaturate to grayscale, then map through one arc hue — shadows to brand-black, mid-tones to the colour, highlights to a bright tint. Remove the background, composite on near-black with a soft coloured halo, and frame with a thin spectral ring. Key the light from the upper-right so the shadow falls to the viewer's left.

Consistency rules

One hue per person, from the eight arc colours, never repeated within a group. Constant eye-line and inter-ocular scale across the set so heads match. Keep the ring thin and the halo subtle. Gold and cyan are still free for new members.
